source.title: Mood Matters: How Syntactic Sensitivity Undermines Safety Alignment
source.authors: Alina Klerings; Jannik Brinkmann; Heiner Stuckenschmidt; Simone Ponzetto

page_placements.theme: Data composition and training objectives shape safety erosion
Surface wording, syntax and obfuscation change refusal

record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests robustness of harmful-request refusal under a different intervention—syntactic reformulation—and evaluates whether deep alignment changes that vulnerability. It does not reproduce the cited fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates syntactic reformulations, causal steering of syntax-sensitive features, post-training data distributions, and syntax-diverse SFT. These are not tests of few-example harmful/benign fine-tuning, per-token KL concentration, compliant prefixes, suffixes, or decoding changes. Results about syntactic reformulation and steering are therefore recorded under fits_no_version unless they directly test V7. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: One appendix result bears on V7. The study evaluates Qi et al.'s deep-alignment Gemma-2-9B checkpoint against a new attack, syntactic reformulation of harmful prompts, and reports that the syntax gap largely persists. The rest of the paper studies syntactic sensitivity of refusal. That is a different construct from the claim's fine-tuning, token-depth, prefill/suffix/decoding and parameter-localization versions, so those results go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that refusal is partly conditioned on superficial syntactic cues (imperative form) rather than harmfulness alone. They trace this to imperative-biased post-training data, and treat syntax-diverse safety SFT as a causal probe rather than a general fix. They also state that existing defenses, deep alignment and circuit breakers, do not mitigate syntactic vulnerability; the paraphrase should add this.
record.recipe_differences: Uses parallel syntactic reformulations, ASR@10, causal mediation/SAE feature steering, and syntax-diverse SFT; it does not reproduce the cited harmful/benign fine-tuning recipe or per-token KL/prefix experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with syntax form; the largest ASR increase differs by model. The deep-alignment checkpoint reduces but does not eliminate the syntax gap. Steering effects vary by feature, prompt type, and steering direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Worst-case syntactic reformulation (conditional form for all models) raises ASR@10 by +15% to +71% over the imperative baseline across 16 instruction-tuned models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal in aligned models depends on the prompt's syntactic form, not only on harmful intent.

fits_no_version.finding: Centroid harmfulness probes keep about 70% accuracy across syntax forms while ASR varies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harm recognition stays intact across syntax forms even when refusal fails.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering imperative/instruction SAE features induces refusal (97–100% on harmful prompts) and partly suppresses it. Random latents induce refusal in about 18% of cases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Upstream syntax features causally gate refusal.
Post-training data is syntactically biased toward the imperative mood.

fits_no_version.finding: SFT of a base model with syntax-diverse safety data cuts non-imperative ASR@10 (e.g. conditional 0.85 to 0.08). Imperative ASR rises from 0.00 to 0.23.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Syntactic diversity in safety data reduces syntax-conditioned refusal failure.

fits_no_version.finding: Imperative phrasing gives near-zero refusal on clearly benign No-Robots prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The imperative mood alone does not trigger refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Circuit breakers fire for imperative harmful prompts. Non-imperative variants mostly get ordinary refusal instead.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-level defenses behave differently across syntactic forms.

record.problems: Behavioral evaluation is limited to 100 harmful and 100 benign English prompts. The authors report WildGuard-human agreement of 91.7% and Cohen’s Kappa of 83.4 based on 120 manually annotated responses. The core behavioral results use ASR@10, and the manually inspected harmful outputs are shortened. Feature labels are automatically generated and treated by the authors as heuristic. Some additional stage-specific plots are not numerically transcribed in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5's ASR@10 values by post-training stage and syntax are not individually extracted because the figure text does not reliably associate each plotted value with a checkpoint and syntax condition. Table 8's additional corpus subset and voice-distribution entries are omitted; Table 2's stage-level imperative shares are retained. Table 13's alternative SAE-feature results are omitted to prioritize the primary feature, controls, and tested model extensions.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning of aligned models on harmful examples.
No benign fine-tuning of safety-trained models. The syntax-diverse SFT starts from a base model.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes. Syntactic reformulation changes the prompt, not the response opening.
No weight or rank localization. SAE feature steering acts on activations, not a small set of parameters.
The study links syntax-conditioned refusal to imperative-biased data, not first-token shallowness to data or objective.

The study does not measure whether deep alignment spreads safety across response positions. It does not re-test robustness to prefill or fine-tuning attacks; it only asserts these are addressed, citing Qi et al. Only one model (Gemma-2 9B) was tested.

record.verdict_notes: The only claim-relevant evidence is appendix §D.2. It is one model and one ∆max number per condition, with no CI for the deep-alignment comparison. The study does not itself verify that deep alignment resists prefill or fine-tuning attacks. The steering rows deliberately induce behaviour, so they cannot be counted as rates of the behaviour arising on its own. The study is not an original source, though it evaluates an original source's released checkpoint.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune safety-trained models on a few to a few hundred harmful examples or measure resulting harmful compliance.
Does not test ordinary or carefully selected benign instruction fine-tuning on a safety-trained model.
Does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL divergence or response-position concentration.
Tests syntactic reformulations, not compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
Steers activation features, but does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Tests whether syntactic diversity in safety data changes syntax-conditioned refusal, not whether data or objectives cause first-token shallowness.

Evaluates a deep-alignment checkpoint against syntactic vulnerability, but does not measure whether safety training spreads across response-token positions or test its robustness to prefills, suffixes, and decoding changes. Syntax-diverse SFT is also tested, but it is not a test of spreading safety beyond initial response tokens.

rows.subject: 16 instruction-tuned models (aggregate; eight families, two sizes each)
rows.operation_detail: Compared imperative harmful prompts with the most vulnerable of seven syntactic reformulations using ASR@10.
rows.measure: Change in ASR@10 from imperative baseline
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval estimated by paired bootstrap over prompts, 10k resamples; paper says vulnerability is robust across all 16 models
rows.note: Aggregate range is explicitly reported in the text; individual model values are not transcribed from the plots.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Compared syntactic vulnerability with and without deep-alignment post-training.

conditions.value: change in maximum ASR@10 versus imperative baseline

rows.measure: Maximum ASR@10 gap across syntax forms
rows.note: The paper describes only a minor decrease and says the syntax gap persists.
rows.check: Baseline and value are ∆max ASR@10 (worst syntax form minus imperative baseline), not absolute ASR: 25% without and 19% with deep alignment. The study gives no absolute ASR for the deep-alignment checkpoint and no uncertainty. The authors call it 'only a minor decrease' and say the gap persists.

relationships.condition: Gemma-2-9B deep-alignment checkpoint (Qi et al.) on JBB harmful prompts rephrased into non-imperative syntax, ASR@10 judged by WildGuard
relationships.reason: r02: deep alignment cuts the worst-case syntax ASR gap only from 25% to 19%. The authors say the gap persists, so the deepening fix does not extend to syntactic reformulation.
relationships.display_finding: The worst-case attack success gap from non-imperative rephrasing shrank only from 25% to 19%, and the authors say the gap persists.

relation.reason: The study directly compares Gemma-2 9B with and without deep alignment and measures whether the defense withstands syntactic reformulation.

tranche.reason: §D.2 evaluates the existing deep-alignment defense in a new attack setting, syntactic reformulation, and reports a result bearing on V7.

source_check.notes: §D.2 reports gaps relative to imperative prompts, not absolute ASR for the deep-alignment checkpoint. Table 3 uses SFT from a base model; the authors present syntax diversification as a causal probe.
